rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing truncation risk. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test whether selectivity separates the clustered middle peaks and co-eluting final pair. The short initial elution window gives ample room for later gradient refinement.

Test the opposite temperature extreme with the same gradient to map selectivity changes before refining the slope. Lower temperature may split the persistent middle cluster differently from the 60 C run.
Retain the favorable 25 C selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the two marginal pairs. The current last peak at 6.37 min leaves room to gain resolution before incurring a time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping a slope close to injection 4 to test a different selectivity lever. This may separate the middle pair without sacrificing the improved late-pair resolution, while shortening retention.

Test a substantially shallower slope to see whether the middle pair separates after an elution-order crossover, while further improving the late pair. Raising the starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Use a shallower gradient with a lower starting fraction to push the middle pair farther through its apparent selectivity crossover. The late pair should retain adequate resolution, with the final peak expected near the unpenalized time window.

Injection 7 achieved the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. The middle pair has little resolution margin, so this tests the speed limit while preserving injection 7 as the benchmark.

Restore the fully resolving gradient duration and raise temperature by one step to seek faster elution through a different lever. This tests whether temperature preserves or improves the critical middle-pair selectivity, with injection 7 retained as the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to 25 C and raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, while making the gradient shallower to protect the critical middle pair. This tests a faster alternative to injection 7 without relying on the unfavorable temperature shift.

At 30 C, test a steeper gradient to improve the final pair, while lowering the starting organic fraction to help preserve middle-pair selectivity. This seeks full resolution with a shorter elution window than injection 7.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a moderately steeper slope to move the middle pair away from its crossover on the faster-eluting side. The late pair’s resolution margin in recent 25 C runs supports exploring this shorter-retention regime.
Shorten injection 12’s gradient by one step to reduce the elution time while retaining its favorable selectivity. Its minimum resolution of 1.91 provides some margin for this speed increase.

Reduce gradient duration by another grid step to seek faster full resolution. Monitor both the middle pair that fell to R 1.96 and the late pair at R 1.79, retaining injection 13 as the faster validated benchmark.

Shorten the gradient one more step to establish the full-resolution speed boundary. The small margins in injection 14 make this a deliberate boundary test; retain its 4.14-minute separation if either critical pair falls below R 1.5.

Back off to the fully resolving 12-minute gradient and test a 5 C temperature increase for faster elution. This isolates temperature’s effect in the high-starting-organic regime while retaining injection 14 as the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Return to 25 C and raise the starting organic fraction one step, using a shallower slope to offset gradient compression. This tests whether a narrower elution window can beat injection 14’s 4.14-minute fully resolved separation.

Test whether a larger temperature shift carries the critical middle pair through its selectivity crossover and restores separation at shorter retention times. Injection 14 remains the fastest validated maximum-score method if this exploratory run loses resolution.

Keep injection 17’s higher starting fraction but reduce the slope to recover its single unresolved middle pair. This tests whether that regime can deliver full resolution with retention competitive with injection 14.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 14 and 15 by lowering the endpoint at the shorter gradient duration. This closely probes the full-resolution boundary while seeking a last-peak time below 4.14 minutes.

Shift the starting fraction down one step while preserving injection 20’s slope to test whether the limiting middle pair gains resolution. This explores a neighboring selectivity window, with injection 14 retained as the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction to check for a faster selectivity window beyond the unresolved pair at phi0 0.40. A shallow slope should limit compression, though early-pair resolution will need close inspection.

Test whether temperature moves the unresolved middle pair at phi0 0.40 through its crossover into a faster fully resolved window. Injection 14 remains the fastest validated maximum-score method, so this is a targeted alternative rather than a replacement.

Return near the fastest validated maximum-score method and test a narrower gradient window with a slightly shallower slope. This should provide more resolution margin than injection 14 while substantially shortening the programmed gradient.

Combine a shallower gradient with 30 C to recover the middle-pair resolution lost in injection 16 while retaining temperature-driven time savings. This final refinement seeks another maximum-score method; injection 14 remains the fastest validated fully resolved separation.
